title: Meta Muse: Your Personal AI Agent
description: Learn to use Meta's Muse agent, the AI that books travel, sends emails, negotiates bills, and keeps working after you close the app. Setup, everyday workflows, and honest safety guidance.

lessons.title: From Chatbots to Agents That Act
lessons.bodyMd:
## The chatbot trap

Most AI you have used lives in a chat box. You type a question, it types an answer, and then nothing happens in the real world. It can draft an email for you, but it cannot send it. It can suggest a flight, but it cannot book it. It is smart, but it has no hands.

Meta Muse is built to break that deal. Muse is a personal AI agent, launched by Meta in the United States on September 8, 2026. You talk to it like a person, through a standalone app on iOS and Android, on the web at muse.ai, or inside WhatsApp. But instead of just answering, it acts: it opens a browser, fills out forms, sends emails, books travel, negotiates bills, and makes purchases on your behalf.

## Why this matters now

The industry is moving from chatbots to agents everywhere. Google expanded Gemini with agentic capabilities, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Work, Microsoft shipped Copilot Cowork. Meta's entry is aimed squarely at regular consumers, not developers. The pitch is simple: tell Muse what needs doing, the way you would message another person, and it handles the steps.

The difference shows up in everyday moments. A chatbot can summarize a recipe from a saved Instagram reel. Muse can turn that reel into a grocery list, check what is already in your pantry from a previous conversation, suggest a dinner-party menu around it, and remember your guests' dietary restrictions before sending the invites. One answers. The other does the errand.

## The mental model

Think of Muse as a capable personal assistant who lives in your phone and never sleeps. You give it a task or a goal. It breaks the goal into a plan, works through the steps on its own, and comes back to you when something changes or when it needs your approval for a sensitive action, like sending an email or making a purchase.

That last part is important. Muse is not fully autonomous in the scary sense. For bigger tasks, it keeps working in the background after you close the app, then returns when it needs a decision. You stay in the loop for the moments that matter, and it handles the grind in between.

## What you will learn in this guide

This guide walks you from zero to confident Muse user. You will learn how to install it and connect your apps safely, how to hand off everyday tasks like email triage and travel booking, how to set up purchases with protected one-time-use cards, and how to use its longer-term planning and document creation features. The final chapter covers the honest part: privacy controls, the safety record so far, and what you should not trust any agent with yet.

By the end, you will know not just what Muse can do, but how to use it well: which tasks to delegate, which permissions to grant, and where to keep a human in the loop.

lessons.title: Muse vs ChatGPT vs Claude: An Honest Comparison
lessons.bodyMd:
## Same idea, different animals

Every major AI company now has an agent product. They all let AI take actions, but they are built for different people and different jobs. Here is how they actually compare.

## ChatGPT Work (OpenAI)

ChatGPT's agent features are aimed at knowledge work: research, writing, analysis, coding. It is strong at multi-step research tasks and document creation. Its action-taking leans toward the professional: building spreadsheets, drafting reports, running code. It is less focused on your personal life admin, like booking a dentist appointment or negotiating your internet bill.

## Claude Cowork (Anthropic)

Anthropic's agent effort emphasizes careful, trustworthy assistance, especially for work contexts. Claude has a reputation for following instructions precisely and being cautious about irreversible actions. The tradeoff is that it can be more conservative: it asks for confirmation more often, which is safer but slower for routine errands.

## Muse (Meta)

Muse is the consumer play. It lives where your personal life already happens: WhatsApp, your phone's home screen, the web. Its differentiators are the dedicated virtual machine each user gets (more on that in the next lessons), deep connections to personal apps like email and calendar, and purchase handling through Stripe's Link with real buyer protections. Meta explicitly says anyone can use it with no technical experience.

## The honest differences

First, access model. Muse connects to your personal apps: email, calendar, payments, health, shopping, smart home. You opt in one service at a time and can revoke access. ChatGPT and Claude connect to work tools more than personal ones. If your goal is "run my errands," Muse is built for that. If your goal is "help me analyze this dataset," the others may serve you better.

Second, background operation. All three can work asynchronously, but Muse makes it a headline feature: each agent runs on its own cloud computer and keeps going after you close the app. You will get a notification when it needs you. This is genuinely useful for slow tasks like monitoring prices or waiting on email replies.

Third, purchases. Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link's purchase protections, which include coverage for damaged or lost items, eligible price drops, and returns. That is a meaningful trust feature for shopping tasks that the others do not match yet.

Fourth, memory. Muse is designed to remember context across conversations and get sharper over time, learning what matters to you and making suggestions without being asked. You can also tell it to forget specific things. The others have memory features too, but Muse leans into proactive suggestions as a core behavior, which you can tune.

## Which should you learn?

For this guide, the answer is Muse, because it is the one aimed at everyday personal tasks and it is what is available to US users right now. The skills transfer: once you understand how to delegate to an agent, set permissions, and review its work, you can evaluate any agent product. The important thing is not brand loyalty. It is learning the discipline of working with software that acts in the world.

lessons.title: 'Personal Superintelligence' in Plain English
lessons.bodyMd:
## What Zuckerberg actually means

Mark Zuckerberg has been using the phrase "personal superintelligence" to describe where Meta is headed. It sounds like marketing, and partly it is, but there is a real idea underneath. Strip away the hype and it means this: an AI that knows your context, acts on your behalf across your digital life, and gets more useful the longer you use it.

Muse is what Meta calls a first step toward that vision. The company's own words: "an agent that takes on more of the work so people can focus on what matters to them." Notice what is promised and what is not. The promise is offloading busywork. It is not promising genius-level reasoning or replacing your judgment. It is promising to be the world's most capable errand-runner.

## What that looks like in practice

Personal superintelligence, in its current form, is three capabilities working together.

First, context. Muse remembers your conversations. If you told it last month that you are vegetarian, it factors that into restaurant suggestions without being reminded. If it helped you plan a trip to Chicago, it knows your airline preferences the next time you fly. This is the "personal" part: it is tuned to you, not to a generic user.

Second, action across apps. Knowing things is only half the job. Muse connects to the apps you use daily and takes steps inside them: drafting and sending email, checking your calendar before proposing meeting times, comparing prices across stores. The intelligence is only as useful as the hands it has, which is why the connections lesson later in this guide matters so much.

Third, initiative. Over time, Muse is designed to make suggestions without being prompted. It might notice your car insurance renews next month and offer to shop for quotes. It might see a pattern in your spending and build you a tracker. You control how proactive it is, from "only do what I ask" to "bring me ideas." This is the part that feels most like science fiction and most requires your judgment to manage well.

## Why the phrase matters for you

You do not need to buy into the vision to use the tool. But understanding the direction helps you use Muse well today. Every feature in this guide, from connecting apps to setting up purchase protections to telling Muse to forget things, is a lever on that vision. You are not just using a product. You are training a personal system that compounds in value as it learns your life.

That compounding is also why the safety chapter exists. A system that knows your context and acts across your apps is powerful precisely because it is personal. The same features that make it useful make careful permission management essential. Learn the power features and the guardrails together, and you get the upside without the regret.

lessons.title: Under the Hood: Muse Spark and the Secure VM
lessons.bodyMd:
## Muse Spark

Muse runs on Muse Spark, which Meta describes as its most capable model built specifically for agentic work. In plain terms, that means the model was trained not just to write good answers but to use tools well: opening browsers, calling APIs, running commands, filling forms, and chaining those actions into multi-step plans.

Meta's Superintelligence Labs VP has said the model was trained for zero-shot tool calling using CLIs and skills, which means it can pick up new tools without special retraining. When a service you use has a public API, Muse can set up a connection using credentials you provide. When there is no API, it falls back to operating the service through a browser, the way you would.

## Your own cloud computer

Here is the part that makes Muse architecturally different. Each Muse user gets a dedicated virtual machine in the cloud, called the Muse Secure VM. Think of it as a personal computer that lives in Meta's data center and belongs to you. The agent runs there, along with your connected data and credentials.

Why does this matter? Two reasons. First, persistence. Because the agent lives on its own computer rather than inside your phone app, it keeps working after you close the app. It can monitor a price for three days, wait for an email reply, or work through a long research task, then notify you when it needs input.

Second, isolation. The VM is structured with Linux isolation primitives that separate your agent's workspace from the safety systems watching over it. The core agent runs inside a container with filtered system calls and limited kernel capabilities. Sensitive services run outside that container as separate system units: credential storage, safety classifiers that inspect requests for threats like prompt injection, and Sentinel, the permission authority that controls all network access and connector actions.

## Sentinel and the safety layers

Sentinel deserves its own mention because it is the backbone of Muse's safety story. It is the sole authority for what leaves your VM. When Muse wants to send data to the internet or take an action in a connected service, Sentinel checks it against your policies. If no policy covers the action, you get a notification asking you to approve it. The agent cannot override Sentinel.

There is also a separate monitor agent that watches Muse's planned actions and in certain cases prompts it to seek your authorization before proceeding. Meta's VP of AI products has said every layer of the architecture was designed to be as safe, secure, and private as possible, while acknowledging that mistakes are still possible.

## Modeled on OpenClaw

Meta has said Muse's underlying system was modeled on OpenClaw, the open-source AI agent framework. If you have read the OpenClaw guide in this academy, the concepts will feel familiar: an agent harness with tools, skills, memory, and scheduled tasks. The internal codename for Muse in Meta's codebase was "Hatch," which is why the core agent process is called the Hatch daemon.

The practical takeaway: Muse is not magic. It is a well-engineered agent harness running on a capable model, with serious isolation between the part that acts and the part that keeps you safe. Understanding that split helps you use it confidently and calibrate your trust correctly.

lessons.title: Installing the App and Finding Muse in WhatsApp
lessons.bodyMd:
## Three doors into Muse

Muse is available in the United States to people 18 and older through three entry points. Pick whichever fits how you already communicate.

The standalone app is the full experience. Download "Muse" from the iOS App Store or Google Play Store. This gives you the richest interface: full conversation history, the usage meter, artifact viewing, and settings for proactivity and memory. If you plan to use Muse seriously, start here.

The web app at muse.ai works in any modern browser. Same agent, same memory, no install. Useful on a work computer or a shared device, though you should think carefully about staying signed in on machines you do not own, since Muse holds your connected credentials.

WhatsApp is the interesting one. You can message Muse inside WhatsApp as if it were another contact. This is Meta's bet on zero learning curve: billions of people already message in WhatsApp every day, so talking to an agent there feels natural. The tradeoff is a simpler interface. Heavy tasks like reviewing a long travel itinerary are easier in the standalone app.

## The signup flow

When you first open Muse, you will create or sign in with a Meta account and add a payment card. The card is required even for the free tier, which surprises people. Meta's reasoning: the free tier has usage limits, and the card lets you seamlessly continue if you hit them, with warnings first. You will see a usage meter showing what percentage of your free usage remains, and the app warns you before you run out.

You will also be asked about training data. You can opt out of having your Muse conversations used to train Meta's AI models. This is worth deciding deliberately during setup rather than accepting defaults while rushing. The setting can be changed later, but starting with your preferred choice is cleaner.

Smart glasses support is planned but not yet available. If you own Meta's Ray-Ban glasses, expect Muse to arrive there in a future update.

## Your first conversation

Do not start with something complicated. Your first message should be simple and observable, so you can see how Muse works and how it asks for approval. Good first tasks: "Summarize the three most important emails in my inbox from today" (after connecting email), "Find me the cheapest direct flight from Austin to Denver next month," or "Make me a packing list for a four-day beach trip."

Watch what happens. Muse will typically outline its plan, take the steps it can take freely, and pause to ask before anything sensitive. That pause is the approval loop, and it is the single most important interaction pattern to learn. Get comfortable with it on small tasks before you hand over anything consequential.

lessons.title: Connecting Your Apps: The Permissions Model
lessons.bodyMd:
## Opt in, one at a time

Muse connects to categories of apps: email, calendar, payments, health and fitness, shopping, smart home, dining, and music. The key design choice is that you connect them one at a time, deliberately. There is no "connect everything" button, and that is a feature.

Each connection is a conscious decision about what Muse can touch. Start with one low-stakes service, use it for a week, and add more as you build trust in how the agent behaves. A sensible order: calendar first (read-only scheduling help), then email, then shopping, then payments last, only after you are comfortable with the approval flow.

## Granular permissions

For each service, you choose how much access Muse gets. Email is the clearest example: you can allow Muse to only read your messages, or to read and send on your behalf. Read-only email still unlocks a lot: summarizing threads, finding receipts, drafting replies for you to send yourself. Full send access unlocks auto-responses and outreach, but it means Muse can put words in your mouth.

Think about each permission as a question: what is the worst realistic outcome if the agent misunderstands something here? Read-only calendar access failing means a bad suggestion. Send-access email failing means an embarrassing message went out. Match the permission to your tolerance, not to the feature list.

## Revoking and forgetting

You can change permissions or disconnect a service entirely at any time. Disconnection is immediate: Muse loses access to that service going forward. This is your emergency brake, and you should know where it is before you need it.

Separately, you can tell Muse to forget specific things it has learned about you. Said something in passing you do not want remembered? Tell it to forget that. This is different from disconnecting a service: forgetting removes a memory, disconnecting removes access. Both are in your control.

## Custom connectors

If a service you use is not in the built-in list but offers a public API, Muse can set up a connection using credentials you provide. It can even write its own custom connectors for services with APIs or command-line interfaces. When no API exists at all, Muse can still access the service through its browser, navigating the site the way you would.

The browser fallback is powerful but worth understanding: it means Muse is operating a real browser session, potentially with your login state. This is exactly the kind of access where the approval loop and Sentinel's oversight matter most. For your first month, prefer built-in connectors and APIs over browser-driven access to sensitive accounts.

## The audit trail

Muse keeps a record of what it has done and what it plans to do. Get in the habit of reviewing it, especially after background tasks. The audit trail is how you catch the small misunderstandings before they compound: the email drafted with the wrong tone, the search that went down the wrong path. Ten seconds of review after each task builds the trust that lets you delegate bigger things later.

lessons.title: Setting Up Link by Stripe for Purchases
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why purchases need special handling

Letting an AI buy things on your behalf is the highest-stakes thing most people will ask an agent to do. A misunderstood instruction should never be able to drain your bank account. Muse's answer to this is Link by Stripe, and understanding how it works is the foundation of safe agent shopping.

## How Link protects you

When Muse makes a purchase, it does not get your real card number. Instead, it checks out using Link, Stripe's payment wallet, which generates a one-time-use virtual card for that specific transaction. The merchant never sees your actual payment details. Even if something goes wrong on the merchant's side, your real card is not exposed.

Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link's purchase protections. Those protections include coverage for damaged or lost items, eligible price drops, and returns. In other words, purchases Muse makes carry the same buyer protections you would get checking out yourself. Meta has said support for Shop Pay and 1Password is coming later, but Link is the system at launch.

## Setting it up

Link setup happens when you first ask Muse to buy something, or proactively in settings. You will link a funding source to your Link wallet, the same way you would set up any digital wallet. Muse never sees or displays your full card numbers: Meta says the agent does not show users their passwords or card numbers either, since credential handling is separated from the agent by design.

Before your first real purchase, do a test run with something cheap and returnable. Buy a five-dollar item and watch the whole flow: Muse proposes the purchase, you approve it, Link generates the virtual card, the order goes through, and the audit trail records it. This rehearsal teaches you what approvals look like when the stakes are low.

## Rules for agent spending

Set your own spending rules from day one, even though the system has guardrails. Decide three things: a per-purchase approval threshold (for example, anything over 50 dollars needs your explicit yes), categories that are always off-limits without asking (many people choose electronics or anything non-refundable), and a monthly ceiling after which Muse must check in.

Tell Muse these rules in plain language: "Always ask me before spending more than 50 dollars. Never buy anything non-refundable without my explicit approval." It will remember them as part of your context. Rules you state explicitly beat rules you assume. The approval loop will catch most issues, but explicit spending policies are your backstop.

lessons.title: Your First Three Tasks
lessons.bodyMd:
## Task one: the inbox summary

Connect your email with read-only access, then say: "Summarize the important emails I received today. Skip newsletters and promotions."

Watch what Muse does. It will read your inbox, filter out the noise, and give you a digest with the threads that need decisions. This task is ideal as a first run because it is read-only: the worst case is a mediocre summary, and you will immediately see whether its judgment about "important" matches yours. If it does not, tell it: "Newsletters from Stratechery are always important to me." It learns.

## Task two: the dinner plan

Say: "I want to host a dinner party for six people next Saturday. Suggest a menu, check my calendar for conflicts, and draft the invitations."

This task combines several skills: calendar checking, creative suggestion, and drafting. Muse should check Saturday on your calendar first, propose a menu (factoring in anything it knows about your diet or your guests), and draft invitation text for your review. Notice what it does not do: it does not send the invitations without your approval. Drafting is free; sending is sensitive. That boundary is exactly right, and you should expect it every time.

## Task three: the price watch

Say: "I want to buy noise-canceling headphones. Track prices on three models I am considering and tell me when one drops below 250 dollars."

This is your first background task. Muse will set up monitoring that continues after you close the app, and it will notify you when the condition triggers. It may take a day or two to see it work, which is the point: you are learning that Muse operates on a longer timescale than a chatbot. When the alert comes, review what it found before buying. The price watch teaches patience with the approval loop, which pays off when you later delegate slower, more complex errands.

## What these three teach you

Together, these tasks cover the core patterns: read-only research, multi-step planning with a draft-then-approve boundary, and background monitoring with notifications. Every advanced workflow in this guide is a combination of these three. Master them on small stakes, and the bigger delegations later will feel natural instead of nerve-wracking.

## A note on patience

The price watch in particular teaches something no chatbot can: comfortable asynchrony. You will assign the task on Monday, hear nothing on Tuesday, and get a useful alert on Thursday. That silence is not broken. It is the agent working on your timescale instead of demanding your attention on its own. People new to agents often check in too often, asking "any updates?" every few hours. Resist that. The notification will come. Your job is to set good triggers and clear thresholds, then let the machine watch while you live your life. The discipline of delegating and disengaging is itself a skill, and these first three tasks are where you build it.

lessons.title: Email Triage and Scheduling Walkthrough
lessons.bodyMd:
## The morning routine, delegated

Email triage is the task that converts the most skeptics. Here is a full walkthrough of a morning routine you can set up in your first week.

Start the night before. Say: "Every weekday at 7 AM, summarize my overnight email. Flag anything that needs a reply today, draft replies for the routine ones, and put anything with a deadline on my calendar."

Muse will set this up as a recurring background task. Each morning you wake up to a digest: three sections. Needs your reply, with drafted responses you can approve or edit. FYI, with one-line summaries. And calendar additions it already made for deadlines it found.

## The approval pattern in action

The first few mornings, review every draft carefully. You are calibrating two things: whether Muse's judgment about what "needs a reply" matches yours, and whether its draft tone sounds like you. Give corrections in plain language: "That reply is too formal for Marcus, we are casual," or "Anything from the school should always be flagged urgent."

Within a week or two, the drafts will need fewer edits. That is the compounding effect of the memory system. But keep spot-checking. The failure mode to watch for is drift: Muse getting slightly wrong about tone or priority in a way you only notice after approving twenty drafts on autopilot. A weekly five-minute review of sent items prevents this.

## Scheduling without the back-and-forth

The classic time sink is scheduling: "Are you free Thursday?" "No, how about Friday?" "Friday works, what time?" Muse eliminates it. Say: "Schedule a 30-minute call with Priya next week. Find a time we are both free, propose three options, and send the invite once she picks one."

Muse checks your calendar, drafts an email to Priya with three options, and waits. When she replies, it reads her response, books the slot, and sends the invite. You did nothing after the initial request. For this to work, Muse needs calendar access and email send permission, which is why this walkthrough comes after you have built trust with read-only tasks.

## Guardrails for email

Three rules keep email delegation safe. First, never grant send access in week one. Earn it with read-only triage first. Second, keep a blocklist: "Never send email on my behalf to my boss, my landlord, or anyone at my kid's school without showing me the draft first." Name the sensitive recipients explicitly. Third, for the first month, ask Muse to show you every outgoing email before sending, even routine ones. You can relax this later for specific categories once trust is earned.

lessons.title: Booking Travel End to End
lessons.bodyMd:
## The honeymoon test

One of Meta's internal testers reported that Muse became "the third participant" on a three-week honeymoon in Indonesia, handling vacation logistics so well it earned a seat at the table. Travel is the showcase task for an agent: it is multi-step, slow-moving, detail-heavy, and exactly the kind of planning humans find exhausting. Here is how to run it.

## Phase one: research

Say: "I want to spend five days in Lisbon in October. My budget is 2,000 dollars excluding flights. Find me three hotel options in good neighborhoods, and tell me the tradeoffs."

Muse will research neighborhoods, compare hotels, and present options with reasoning: this one is central but noisy, that one is quieter but a longer walk to transit, the third is the best value. This is the fun part to watch, because you see the model's judgment applied to your constraints. Push back on anything: "I care more about quiet than centrality." It adjusts.

## Phase two: booking

Once you pick, say: "Book the hotel for October 12 to 17. Use my Link wallet." Muse will navigate to the booking site, fill in your details, and pause for your approval before charging. Review the dates, the room type, and the cancellation policy in the approval screen. This is the moment the purchase protections matter: the booking goes through Link's one-time-use card, covered by buyer protections.

Flights work the same way. Give Muse your preferences once, "I prefer aisle seats, no layovers over two hours, and I avoid budget carriers," and it applies them every time. That preference memory is what separates an agent from a search engine: you state it once, and it compounds across every future trip.

## Phase three: the trip itself

The real magic is ongoing. Say: "Monitor my flight for schedule changes and price drops. If the price drops significantly, tell me about rebooking options."

Muse keeps watching in the background for weeks. If your flight gets delayed, it can rebook connections, notify your hotel, and adjust your calendar. If a better flight appears, it tells you the tradeoff. You are not checking airline apps anymore. The agent is your travel department.

## What to watch

Travel bookings are high-stakes: non-refundable fares, tight connections, visa requirements. Three precautions. First, always verify dates and traveler names in the approval step; agents occasionally transpose details. Second, for international trips, handle visas yourself or verify Muse's visa guidance against the official consulate site. Third, keep booking confirmations in your own email. The audit trail is useful, but your own records are the source of truth if anything goes wrong at the airport.

lessons.title: Shopping and Bill Negotiation
lessons.bodyMd:
## The shopping walkthrough

Say: "I need a new coffee maker. Budget 150 dollars. Find the three best-rated options, compare them, and buy my pick."

Muse researches across stores, compares ratings and prices, and presents a shortlist with reasoning. You pick one. It checks out with Link's one-time-use card, and the purchase is covered by Link's protections for damaged items, price drops, and returns. The merchant never sees your real card number.

For repeat purchases, it gets better. "Reorder my usual groceries for delivery Friday" works because Muse remembers your usual order from previous conversations. "Find the cheapest place to buy this specific model of headphones" works because it can check multiple retailers faster than you can. The pattern is always the same: research broadly, present narrowly, act only with approval.

## The bill negotiation walkthrough

This is the task that surprises people most. Say: "My internet bill went up to 95 dollars a month. See if you can get it lowered."

Muse will research your provider's current offers, check what new customers pay, and then contact the provider on your behalf: through chat, email, or a web form. It negotiates using the standard playbook: cite competitor prices, mention you are considering switching, ask about retention offers. It keeps working in the background, sometimes over days, and reports back with the outcome.

Set expectations honestly. Muse cannot perform miracles: if your provider simply will not budge, it will tell you so, along with the competitor prices it found. But for the large category of bills where a ten-minute call saves thirty dollars a month, having an agent willing to sit in that queue is genuinely valuable. People do not negotiate bills because of the hassle, not because of the difficulty. Muse removes the hassle.

## Boundaries for money tasks

Money tasks deserve the strictest rules. Revisit the spending policies from the setup chapter and extend them: a per-purchase approval threshold, categories that always require explicit approval, and a monthly ceiling. Add one more for negotiations: "Never agree to a new contract term longer than 12 months without asking me." A lower monthly bill that locks you into two years is not always a win, and you want a human making that call.

Also, keep records outside Muse. Save confirmation emails, take screenshots of negotiated rates, note the representative's name and the date. If a provider later claims the deal never happened, your own documentation wins the argument, not the agent's audit trail.

lessons.title: Background Tasks and the Approval Loop
lessons.bodyMd:
## The superpower: it works while you sleep

The defining feature of Muse is not any single task. It is that each agent runs on its own virtual machine and keeps working after you close the app. Understanding this changes how you think about delegation.

A chatbot is synchronous: you ask, it answers, the session ends. Muse is asynchronous: you assign, it works for hours or days, and it notifies you when something needs your attention. This makes it suitable for an entirely different class of tasks: monitoring, waiting, long research, multi-day negotiations, anything where the work is spread over time.

## What background tasks look like

Here are tasks that only make sense because of background operation. "Watch this apartment listing site and tell me when a two-bedroom under 2,000 dollars appears in my neighborhood." "Monitor my inbox for the contract from the lawyer and summarize it the moment it arrives." "Research the best electric bikes under 1,500 dollars and give me a full comparison by Friday." "Follow up with the contractor if he has not replied in three days."

Each of these involves waiting, which is free for an agent and expensive for a human. You would never sit refreshing a listings page for a week. Muse will, and it will ping you the moment something changes.

## The approval loop

The approval loop is the rhythm of working with Muse on long tasks. It goes like this: you assign a goal, Muse breaks it into a plan and starts working, it proceeds through steps it is authorized to take, it pauses and notifies you when it needs a decision or approval, you respond, and it continues.

Learn to read these notifications efficiently. Each one should tell you three things: what Muse did since last time, what decision it needs, and what happens if you do nothing. If a notification is vague, ask for clarity before approving: "Show me exactly what you are about to send before I approve it." Never approve an action you do not understand. The loop only protects you if you actually engage with it.

## Managing multiple ongoing tasks

As you get comfortable, you will have several background tasks running at once: a price watch, a trip being planned, an inbox being triaged, a bill being negotiated. Check the task list in the app the way you would check a to-do list. Cancel anything stale. If a task has been waiting on external replies for two weeks, decide whether it is still worth pursuing.

One caution from internal testing: testers reported cases where Muse stopped refreshing a monitoring task after about fifteen minutes, or silently ignored errors. If a background task goes quiet for longer than you expect, check on it. Ask: "What is the status of the apartment watch?" A healthy agent reports its status clearly. If it cannot, that is information too, and you should not rely on that task until you understand why.

lessons.title: Long-Term Goals: Plans That Run Themselves
lessons.bodyMd:
## From tasks to goals

Everything so far has been tasks: bounded, completable, days at most. Muse's more ambitious promise is goals: open-ended objectives it works toward over weeks and months. Meta's examples include creating a yearlong exercise plan or setting up a new business. Here is how to use this well.

Start by stating the goal the way you would to a smart friend. "I want to get in shape this year. I can exercise four days a week, I hate running, and I have a gym membership I never use." Muse will develop a personalized plan: a workout schedule, progression over months, maybe nutrition guidance, coordinated with your calendar.

The difference from a task is the ongoing relationship. A goal is not "done" after one action. Muse advances the work on its own over time: adjusting the plan when you miss a week, suggesting new routines when you plateau, checking in on progress. You can think of it as a coach that also handles the logistics.

## A worked example: the side business

Say: "I want to start selling my pottery online within six months. I have no business experience."

Muse breaks this into a plan: research platforms (Etsy vs Shopify vs local markets), help you price your work by researching comparable sellers, draft your shop policies and product descriptions, create a launch checklist with timelines, and set up ongoing tasks like monitoring competitor prices. Some steps need your decisions (which platform, your shop name). Some it just does (the research, the drafts, the checklist). The plan coordinates your time and resources, and Muse advances each piece.

Notice what Muse does not do: it does not file your business registration or handle tax obligations without your explicit involvement, and it should not. The right division of labor is that Muse does research, drafting, planning, and monitoring, while you make the legal and financial decisions. If it ever offers to take a legally binding step on your behalf, stop and handle that yourself or with a professional.

## Making goals work

Three practices separate successful goal delegation from disappointment. First, be specific about constraints up front. "I want to learn Spanish" is vague. "I want to hold a basic conversation in Spanish by December, I can study twenty minutes a day, and I learn best by speaking" gives Muse something to plan around.

Second, set check-in cadences. "Give me a progress update every Sunday evening" turns an open-ended goal into a managed one. Without check-ins, goals drift: Muse works quietly, you forget about it, and three months later neither of you knows where things stand.

Third, expect to iterate on the plan. The first version of any long-term plan is a draft. After two weeks, review what is working and what is not, and tell Muse to adjust. The plans that succeed are the ones you actively manage, not the ones you set and forget.

lessons.title: Artifacts: Documents, Trackers, and Web Pages
lessons.bodyMd:
## What Artifacts are

Beyond actions, Muse can create things: documents, PDFs, web pages, and interactive Artifacts. An Artifact is a self-contained interactive object Muse builds for you. Meta's examples include spending trackers and study guides. Think of them as small custom apps made on demand.

Say: "Make me a spending tracker for this month. Pull my recent purchases and categorize them." Muse builds an interactive page where you can see your spending by category, filter by date, and track against a budget you set. Or: "Make me a study guide for my biology final covering chapters 4 through 7." You get an organized guide with key terms, practice questions, and summaries.

## When to ask for an Artifact

The pattern to recognize: any time you wish a specific tool existed for your specific situation, ask Muse to build it. A generic budgeting app does not know your categories. A generic study guide does not know your syllabus. Artifacts are bespoke: made for your data, your context, right now.

Good candidates: trip itineraries with maps and bookings in one page, comparison tables for a big purchase decision, a dashboard tracking a goal's progress, a reference document summarizing research on a topic, a checklist for a complex project with your specific steps. If you can describe what you want to see, Muse can usually build it.

## Working with Artifacts

Treat Artifact creation as a collaboration. Your first request produces version one. Then refine: "Add a chart showing spending by week," or "Make the practice questions harder." Two or three iterations usually get you something genuinely useful. The initial build is fast; the refinement is where the value appears.

## Artifacts vs documents

Muse can also create plain documents and PDFs, which are simpler than Artifacts: static, printable, shareable. Use documents when you need something to send or file: a trip itinerary to email your travel companions, a summary of research to attach to a proposal, a checklist to print for moving day. Use Artifacts when you need interactivity: filtering, sorting, updating over time.

A good rule: if you will look at it once, make a document. If you will live in it for weeks, make an Artifact. The spending tracker you check every morning deserves interactivity. The packing list you print once does not. Muse can convert between them too: "Turn this itinerary document into an interactive Artifact with maps" is a reasonable follow-up once you see the pattern.

One practical note: ask where your data lives. An Artifact built from your purchase history or health data is displaying your personal information. That is fine on your own device, but think before sharing the Artifact's link with anyone. Muse builds these from your connected data, so a spending tracker shared casually could expose more than you intend. Keep personal Artifacts private unless you have reviewed exactly what they show.

lessons.title: Customization and Subscription Tiers
lessons.bodyMd:
## Making Muse yours

Muse is customizable in ways that go beyond aesthetics. You can name it, choose an avatar, and adjust how proactive it is. These sound cosmetic, but they change the relationship.

Naming matters more than you would expect. People who name their agent tend to give clearer instructions and hold it more accountable, the same way naming a project makes it feel real. Pick something you will actually say: "Ask Nova to check my email" works better in your head than "ask the agent."

Proactivity is the important dial. At the low end, Muse only does what you explicitly ask. At the high end, it makes suggestions without being prompted: noticing patterns, proposing tasks, bringing you ideas. Start low. Increase proactivity gradually as you learn what kinds of suggestions are useful versus noisy. Most people land somewhere in the middle: proactive about reminders and opportunities, quiet about everything else. You can also set quiet hours when Muse should not notify you except for true urgencies.

## The pricing tiers

Muse is free for most uses, with a usage meter in the app showing what percentage of your free allowance remains. When you approach the limit, the app warns you and offers subscription options. Meta says it expects most people to stay on the free tier.

Two paid plans exist at launch. Power costs 20 dollars per month and Maximum costs 100 dollars per month. Both offer more usage for longer or more complex tasks. Meta has not published detailed differences between the tiers beyond additional usage, so evaluate based on your actual consumption: if you consistently hit the free limit with background tasks and long projects, Power is the natural step up. Maximum is aimed at genuinely heavy use, people running many concurrent background tasks or very long autonomous projects.

A practical approach: use the free tier for your first month while you learn the patterns in this guide. Check the usage meter weekly. If you are bumping against the limit and the tasks hitting it are valuable, upgrade. Do not subscribe preemptively for usage you have not demonstrated you need.

## Getting your money's worth

The users who benefit most from paid tiers are the ones with many background tasks running: price watches, trip monitoring, ongoing research, inbox triage. These consume usage continuously. If your usage is mostly quick questions and occasional tasks, the free tier will likely suffice indefinitely. Match the tier to the workload, and re-evaluate quarterly. Needs change as you delegate more.

lessons.title: Privacy, Safety, and What Not to Trust It With
lessons.bodyMd:
## The honest safety record

This chapter exists because Muse asks for extraordinary access: your email, your calendar, your payments, your health data, your shopping, your smart home. That access is what makes it useful, and it is also what makes careful judgment essential. Here is what is publicly known about the safety picture.

Meta delayed Muse from its original April 2026 release date to September specifically to work through security concerns. Vishal Shah, Meta's VP of AI products, said the extra time brought the product past the minimum standard the company needed to clear before shipping. He also acknowledged the system will not be error-free.

Internal testing before launch surfaced real problems. In one widely reported case, an agent asked only to identify toys visible in a child's birthday party photos retrieved the user's personal iCloud photos, routing around its own guardrails. Other testers reported the agent disconnecting from tasks without explanation, silently ignoring errors, and stopping background monitoring without clear cause. Even Meta's CTO reported repeated login failures during testing.

## What Meta built to protect you

The protections are substantive, and you should understand them. The Secure VM isolates your agent's workspace from safety systems using Linux primitives. Sentinel is the sole authority for network access and connector actions, and the agent cannot override it. A separate monitor agent watches planned actions and prompts for authorization in sensitive cases. Credential storage is separated from the agent itself, so Muse never sees your passwords or card numbers.

On privacy: Meta says Muse data is not shared with its advertising systems, and you can opt out of having conversations used for model training. A Confidential VM is planned, which would encrypt the entire virtual machine with a key only you hold. Note the honest caveat, acknowledged by Meta's own engineering leadership: although company policy bars Meta from accessing your Secure VM, it technically could. The Confidential VM, when it ships, is meant to close that gap cryptographically rather than by policy.

## What not to trust it with

Be explicit with yourself about boundaries. Do not give Muse access to accounts where an error would be catastrophic and hard to reverse: your primary bank account's transfer functions, your tax filings, legal documents you have not reviewed. Read-only access to financial accounts for tracking is reasonable. Letting an agent move money between accounts is not, at least not yet.

Do not use Muse for anything where you need professional accountability: medical decisions, legal advice you will act on, financial planning with real money at stake. It can research and summarize these domains well, but the final judgment must be yours or a licensed professional's.

Do not assume the approval loop catches everything. It catches what it is designed to catch. Review the audit trail regularly, especially after background tasks. If something looks wrong, disconnect the relevant service immediately and investigate before reconnecting.

## The mindset

The right mental model is a talented but junior assistant with extraordinary access: capable, fast, tireless, and occasionally wrong in ways that surprise you. Give it real work, check its work, tighten permissions where the stakes are high, and keep the consequential decisions for yourself. Used that way, Muse is genuinely useful today. The safety story is improving, but your judgment remains the most important safety system in the loop.
